notes:
Classification & nomenclature

  • Haloalkanes: R–X (sp$^3$ C–X). Haloarenes: Ar–X (sp$^2$ C–X, X directly on ring). Classified as primary, secondary, tertiary by the carbon bearing X; also allylic (C=C–C–X) and benzylic (Ar–C–X).
  • C–X bond length: C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I (increases down the group); bond enthalpy decreases down the group (C–F strongest).

Preparation

  • From alcohols: ROH + HX (ZnCl$_2$/conc. HCl — Lucas test), ROH + PCl$_5$/PCl$_3$/SOCl$_2$ (SOCl$_2$ best, by-products gaseous).
  • From alkenes: HX addition (Markovnikov; peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov only with HBr).
  • Haloarenes: electrophilic substitution (X$_2$/Fe or FeX$_3$) or from diazonium salts (Sandmeyer/Balz-Schiemann).

Physical properties

  • Density increases with number and size of halogens; CHI$_3$, CH$_2$I$_2$, CHBr$_3$ denser than water. Boiling point: RI > RBr > RCl > RF for same R (van der Waals ↑ with size); branching lowers b.p.
  • Haloalkanes are weakly polar but insoluble in water (cannot H-bond with water; break existing H-bonds).

Reactions of haloalkanes

ReactionProduct
Nucleophilic substitution (OH$^-$, CN$^-$, NH$_3$, alkoxide)alcohol, nitrile, amine, ether
Elimination (alc. KOH, heat)alkene (Saytzeff product major)
With Mg in dry etherGrignard reagent RMgX
Wurtz reaction (Na, dry ether)symmetrical alkane R–R
  • S$_N$2: one-step, backside attack, inversion of configuration, rate ∝ [RX][Nu$^-$]; favoured by methyl > 1° > 2° (3° hindered).
  • S$_N$1: two-step via carbocation, racemisation, rate ∝ [RX] only; favoured by 3° (stable carbocation) > 2° > 1°; polar protic solvent helps.

Haloarenes: low reactivity

  • Resonance gives C–X partial double-bond character (shorter, stronger bond); sp$^2$ carbon; ring is electron-rich (repels Nu$^-$); phenyl cation destabilised.
  • Undergo electrophilic substitution slowly (X is o,p-directing but deactivating due to –I > +R).
  • Nucleophilic substitution needs harsh conditions (high T, P, NaOH, e.g. chlorobenzene → phenol at 623 K, 300 atm) or is aided by electron-withdrawing (–NO$_2$) groups at o/p positions.

Important named compounds

  • DDT — insecticide (banned, non-biodegradable); Freons (CFCs) — refrigerants, deplete ozone; Iodoform — antiseptic; Chloroform — anaesthetic (kept in dark bottles, stored with 1% ethanol to prevent oxidation to poisonous COCl$_2$, phosgene).

Exam tip

KCET asks 2–3 questions: S$_N$1 vs S$_N$2 conditions, why haloarenes are less reactive, and one preparation/named-reaction question. Learn the resonance argument for haloarenes thoroughly.

questions.q: The correct order of boiling points for 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane is
questions.explanation: Van der Waals forces increase with the size/mass of the halogen atom, so b.p. increases from Cl to Br to I for the same alkyl group.
questions.trick: b.p. rises with halogen size (van der Waals): RCl $<$ RBr $<$ RI.

questions.q: Which reaction of an alkyl halide proceeds with inversion of configuration?
questions.explanation: S$_N$2 is a single-step backside attack by the nucleophile, giving Walden inversion at the stereocentre.
questions.trick: Backside attack = inversion; that's S$_N$2, always.

questions.q: Chlorobenzene is less reactive than alkyl chlorides towards nucleophilic substitution mainly because
options: chlorine is a poor leaving group in chlorobenzene
chlorine is more electronegative in the ring
resonance gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character
questions.explanation: Delocalisation of a lone pair of Cl into the ring shortens and strengthens the C–Cl bond and makes the carbon less electrophilic, hindering nucleophilic attack.
questions.trick: Aryl halides: resonance gives C-X partial double bond, kills substitution.

questions.q: Which alkyl halide undergoes S$_N$1 reaction fastest?
questions.explanation: S$_N$1 rate depends on carbocation stability; tertiary carbocations are most stable, so tert-butyl chloride reacts fastest.
questions.trick: S$_N$1 rate follows carbocation stability: 3$^\circ$ fastest.

questions.q: Which of the following is used to convert an alcohol to an alkyl chloride with only gaseous by-products?
questions.explanation: ROH + SOCl$_2$ → RCl + SO$_2$↑ + HCl↑, both by-products escape as gases, giving pure RCl (Darzens process).
questions.trick: SOCl$_2$ on ROH gives only gaseous by-products (SO$_2$, HCl) — cleanest RCl.

questions.q: The Wurtz reaction converts an alkyl halide into
questions.explanation: 2 RX + 2Na $\xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}}$ R–R + 2NaX, giving a symmetrical alkane with double the carbon chain.
questions.trick: Wurtz: 2RX + 2Na $\to$ symmetrical alkane, doubling carbon chain.

questions.q: Iodoform test is a characteristic test for compounds containing the group
questions.explanation: Methyl ketones and secondary alcohols with a CH$_3$CH(OH)– group give a yellow precipitate of CHI$_3$ with I$_2$/NaOH.
questions.trick: Iodoform test $\to$ CH$_3$CO- or CH$_3$CH(OH)- group present.

questions.q: Addition of HBr to propene in the presence of peroxide gives predominantly
questions.explanation: Peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov) applies only to HBr: the bromine adds to the terminal (less substituted) carbon via a free-radical mechanism, giving 1-bromopropane.
questions.trick: Peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov) works only with HBr, Br goes to terminal C.

questions.q: Which of these solvents favours an S$_N$1 mechanism?
questions.explanation: Polar protic solvents (water, alcohols) stabilise the carbocation and the leaving halide ion by solvation, favouring the S$_N$1 pathway.
questions.trick: Polar protic solvent stabilises ions $\to$ favours S$_N$1.

questions.q: Grignard reagents must be prepared and used in
questions.explanation: Grignard reagents (RMgX) react violently with even traces of water/moisture to give alkanes, so anhydrous ether is essential.
questions.trick: Grignard reagents demand bone-dry ether; water destroys them instantly.

questions.q: The insecticide DDT is chemically known as
questions.explanation: DDT stands for dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, once widely used as an insecticide but now banned due to non-biodegradability.
questions.trick: DDT = dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, banned, non-biodegradable insecticide.

questions.q: Racemisation is a characteristic feature of which mechanism?
questions.explanation: In S$_N$1 the planar carbocation intermediate is attacked by the nucleophile from either face with nearly equal probability, giving a racemic mixture.
questions.trick: Planar carbocation attacked from both faces $\to$ racemisation = S$_N$1 signature.

questions.q: Chlorobenzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of FeCl$_3$ to give mainly
questions.explanation: Cl is an ortho, para director in electrophilic aromatic substitution due to resonance donation of a lone pair; para is major due to less steric hindrance.
questions.trick: Halogens are o,p-directors (resonance donation); para favoured, less steric clash.

questions.q: The relative rate of S$_N$2 reaction for methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary halides is
options: all react at the same rate
questions.explanation: S$_N$2 requires backside attack; increasing alkyl substitution increases steric hindrance, so methyl halides react fastest and tertiary halides essentially do not undergo S$_N$2.
questions.trick: S$_N$2 rate falls with bulk: methyl $>$ 1$^\circ$ $>$ 2$^\circ$ $>$ 3$^\circ$.

questions.q: Freons are chemically
questions.explanation: Freons (e.g. CCl$_2$F$_2$, Freon-12) are chlorofluorocarbons used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants; they deplete stratospheric ozone.
questions.trick: Freons = CFCs of methane/ethane; refrigerants that deplete ozone.

questions.q: Chloroform is stored in dark-coloured bottles, completely filled, with a little ethanol added, mainly to prevent
options: its oxidation by air and light to the poisonous gas phosgene
questions.explanation: Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in the presence of light to phosgene (COCl$_2$), a poisonous gas; ethanol converts any phosgene formed into harmless diethyl carbonate.
questions.trick: Chloroform + air/light $\to$ toxic phosgene; ethanol traps it, dark bottle prevents it.

questions.q: Which compound would give a precipitate with alcoholic AgNO$_3$ most readily at room temperature?
questions.explanation: tert-Butyl chloride ionises readily (S$_N$1, stable 3° carbocation) at room temperature to release Cl$^-$, which precipitates as AgCl; aryl and vinyl halides do not ionise due to resonance stabilisation of the C–X bond.
questions.trick: Only alkyl halides ionise readily with AgNO$_3$; 3$^\circ$ fastest via stable carbocation.

questions.q: The dipole moment of chlorobenzene is lower than that of cyclohexyl chloride mainly because
options: the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene has partial double-bond character due to resonance, shortening it and reducing charge separation
chlorine is less electronegative in chlorobenzene
cyclohexyl chloride has a longer C–Cl bond
questions.explanation: Resonance in chlorobenzene delocalises the Cl lone pair into the ring, shortening the C–Cl bond and giving it partial double-bond character, which reduces the dipole moment compared with a purely sp$^3$ C–Cl bond.
questions.trick: Resonance shortens aryl C-Cl bond, cutting charge separation and dipole moment.

questions.q: Ethyl bromide on treatment with alcoholic KOH (heat) gives mainly
questions.explanation: Alcoholic KOH favours $\beta$-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) to give an alkene, whereas aqueous KOH favours substitution to give the alcohol.
questions.trick: Alcoholic KOH + heat = elimination (alkene); aqueous KOH = substitution (alcohol).

questions.q: Which of the following alkyl halides would show the fastest S$_N$2 reaction with NaOH?
questions.explanation: Methyl bromide has the least steric hindrance around the electrophilic carbon, so backside attack by OH$^-$ is fastest among these.
questions.trick: Least steric hindrance wins S$_N$2: methyl halide reacts fastest.

questions.q: The correct order of C–X bond length (for a given alkyl group) is
options: all C–X bonds have the same length
questions.explanation: Bond length increases as the halogen atom becomes larger (F < Cl < Br < I in atomic radius), so C–I is the longest and C–F the shortest carbon-halogen bond.
questions.trick: Bond length tracks halogen size: C-F shortest, C-I longest.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an allylic halide?
questions.explanation: An allylic halide has the halogen on the carbon adjacent to a C=C double bond (sp$^3$ carbon next to sp$^2$); CH$_2$=CH–CH$_2$Cl (allyl chloride) fits this, while CH$_2$=CHCl (vinylic) has X directly on the sp$^2$ carbon.
questions.trick: Allylic = X on sp$^3$ carbon next to C=C, not on the sp$^2$ carbon itself.

questions.q: Vinyl halides and aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution mainly because
options: the halogen is attached to an sp$^2$ carbon and the C–X bond has partial double-bond character from resonance
they contain no C–X bond at all
they have no halogen lone pairs
questions.explanation: In both vinyl and aryl halides, the halogen lone pair conjugates with the adjacent $\pi$ system, shortening and strengthening the C–X bond and making it resistant to nucleophilic displacement.
questions.trick: sp$^2$ C-X with resonance double-bond character resists nucleophilic attack (vinyl/aryl).

questions.q: Which alkyl halide, on reaction with alcoholic KOH, would follow Saytzeff's rule to give the more substituted alkene as the major product?
options: 1-chloropropane, giving mainly propene from a single possible elimination
questions.explanation: Saytzeff's rule states that the more substituted (more stable) alkene is the major elimination product; 2-bromobutane can eliminate to give but-1-ene or but-2-ene, and but-2-ene (more substituted) predominates.
questions.trick: Saytzeff: elimination favours the more substituted (more stable) alkene.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why haloalkanes, though polar, are insoluble in water?
options: Haloalkanes cannot form hydrogen bonds with water and instead break the existing hydrogen bonding network of water, which is energetically unfavourable
questions.explanation: To dissolve, a haloalkane molecule would need to break H-bonds between water molecules without forming new ones of comparable strength, making dissolution energetically unfavourable despite the polar C–X bond.
questions.trick: Haloalkanes can't H-bond water and would break water's H-bond network — insoluble.

questions.q: An optically active 2-bromobutane, when heated with aqueous NaOH, gives 2-butanol with predominant inversion but partial racemisation. This mixed behaviour suggests the mechanism is
options: a mixture of S$_N$1 and S$_N$2 pathways operating simultaneously
questions.explanation: A secondary halide is borderline: it can react by both S$_N$2 (pure inversion) and S$_N$1 (racemisation via a planar carbocation), so the product often shows partial inversion and partial racemisation.
questions.trick: Mixed inversion + racemisation = borderline 2$^\circ$ halide, both S$_N$1 and S$_N$2 running.

questions.q: Which combination correctly matches the reagent with its use in converting an alcohol to a haloalkane?
options: dilute HNO$_3$ — converts ROH to RF
Red P + Br$_2$ — converts ROH to RBr via in-situ PBr$_3$
questions.explanation: Red phosphorus reacts with Br$_2$ to generate PBr$_3$ in situ, which then converts the alcohol to the alkyl bromide; this avoids handling the unstable PBr$_3$ directly.
questions.trick: Red P + Br$_2$ generates PBr$_3$ in situ to convert ROH $\to$ RBr.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the reactivity of haloarenes towards electrophilic substitution is correct?
options: Halogen substituents are ortho, para-directing but deactivating (net electron withdrawal by induction exceeds donation by resonance)
Halogen substituents are meta-directing and activating
Halogens have no directing effect on the ring
Halogen substituents are ortho, para-directing and strongly activating
questions.explanation: Halogens donate electron density into the ring by resonance (directing electrophiles to o,p) but withdraw more strongly by induction overall, making the ring less reactive than benzene itself even while directing o,p.
questions.trick: Halogens: o,p-directing by resonance but net deactivating by stronger induction.

questions.q: Which alkyl halide would react fastest with KI in acetone (Finkelstein reaction)?
questions.explanation: The Finkelstein reaction proceeds by S$_N$2; less steric hindrance around the carbon favours faster reaction, so unhindered primary 1-chlorobutane reacts fastest among these, while the very hindered neopentyl halide reacts extremely slowly despite being primary.
questions.trick: Finkelstein is S$_N$2: least hindered primary halide reacts fastest with KI.

questions.q: Which reaction is used to convert chlorobenzene into phenol industrially (Dow process)?
options: Fusion with NaOH at 623 K, 300 atm, followed by acidification
Treatment with dilute HCl at room temperature
questions.explanation: Chlorobenzene is hydrolysed to phenol only under forcing conditions (623 K, 300 atm NaOH) because the C–Cl bond is strengthened by resonance; this harsh requirement is the Dow process.
questions.trick: Dow process: chlorobenzene $\to$ phenol needs harsh 623 K, 300 atm NaOH.

questions.q: A compound C$_4$H$_9$Br reacts with alcoholic KOH to give only one alkene as the elimination product (no isomeric alkenes possible). The compound is most likely
questions.explanation: tert-Butyl bromide, (CH$_3$)$_3$CBr, has only one type of $\beta$-hydrogen (from the three equivalent methyl groups), so elimination gives a single alkene, 2-methylpropene, with no other regiochemical possibility.
questions.trick: Only one type of $\beta$-H (symmetric methyls) $\to$ single elimination alkene possible.

questions.q: Which of the following polyhalogen compounds is used as a general anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Chloroform (trichloromethane) was historically used as an inhalation general anaesthetic, though now largely replaced by safer agents due to toxicity concerns.
questions.trick: Chloroform = classic inhalation general anaesthetic, memorise the pairing.

questions.q: An alkyl halide is treated with sodium metal in the presence of dry ether to give an alkane of double the carbon count. If ethyl bromide is used, the product formed is
questions.explanation: 2 CH$_3$CH$_2$Br + 2Na $\to$ CH$_3$CH$_2$–CH$_2$CH$_3$ (n-butane) + 2NaBr, the Wurtz reaction, doubling the carbon chain of the starting alkyl halide.
questions.trick: Wurtz doubles carbon count: ethyl bromide $\to$ n-butane.

questions.q: Which of the following compounds has zero net dipole moment despite containing polar C–Cl bonds?
questions.explanation: In para-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel by symmetry, giving a net dipole moment of zero, unlike the ortho isomer where the dipoles partially reinforce.
questions.trick: Symmetric para-dichlorobenzene: opposite C-Cl dipoles cancel exactly to zero.

questions.q: Which of the following would undergo the fastest hydrolysis by an S$_N$1 mechanism in aqueous acetone?
questions.explanation: Benzyl chloride ionises readily because the resulting benzylic carbocation is stabilised by resonance delocalisation into the aromatic ring, favouring S$_N$1; aryl and vinyl halides do not ionise due to the strong, resonance-shortened C–Cl bond.
questions.trick: Benzylic C-X ionises fast: resonance-stabilised carbocation favours S$_N$1.

questions.q: Identify the incorrect statement about the S$_N$2 mechanism.
options: It shows retention of configuration at the reacting carbon
It occurs in a single step without any intermediate
It proceeds through a trigonal bipyramidal transition state
The rate depends on the concentration of both the substrate and the nucleophile
questions.explanation: S$_N$2 proceeds with inversion of configuration (Walden inversion) at the carbon centre, not retention, because the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group.
questions.trick: S$_N$2 gives inversion, never retention — check that option first.

questions.q: 3.0 g of a monochloroalkane (C$_n$H$_{2n+1}$Cl) contains 0.71 g of chlorine (Cl, atomic mass 35.5). The approximate mass percentage of chlorine in the compound is used to identify n. What is the mass percentage of Cl?
questions.explanation: Mass % Cl = (0.71/3.0) $\times$ 100 $\approx$ 23.7%, i.e. about 24%.
questions.trick: Mass % Cl = (mass Cl / total mass) $\times$ 100.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct reactivity order of alkyl halides towards a given nucleophile under S$_N$2 conditions?
options: all react at identical rates regardless of the halogen
questions.explanation: Iodide is the best leaving group among halides (weakest C–X bond, most stable leaving anion), so alkyl iodides react fastest in S$_N$2 reactions: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
questions.trick: Best leaving group wins S$_N$2 rate: RI $>$ RBr $>$ RCl $>$ RF.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a correct use of a polyhalogen compound?
options: Freons are used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants
Carbon tetrachloride was used as a fire extinguisher (pyrene) and solvent
Tetrafluoroethene is polymerised to make PTFE (Teflon)
DDT is an effective, completely biodegradable, environmentally safe insecticide
questions.explanation: DDT is actually non-biodegradable and persists in the environment and food chains, which is why it has been banned in many countries despite its earlier effectiveness as an insecticide.
questions.trick: DDT is non-biodegradable, not eco-safe — a common trick 'false' option.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the preparation of Grignard reagents from aryl halides is correct?
options: Only alkyl halides with more than 10 carbons form Grignard reagents
Aryl halides such as bromobenzene can react with Mg in dry ether to form aryl magnesium halides, e.g. C$_6$H$_5$MgBr
Aryl halides can only form Grignard reagents in aqueous medium
Aryl halides never react with Mg under any conditions
questions.explanation: Unlike nucleophilic substitution (which fails on aryl halides), Grignard reagent formation is an oxidative insertion of Mg into the C–X bond and works for aryl halides too, giving aryl magnesium halides like phenylmagnesium bromide.
questions.trick: Grignard formation is Mg insertion into C-X; works on aryl halides too.
